domain_label: Plated Jewelry — Constructing the Coherent 6-SKU Launch Assortment
purpose: A method for turning kb1's ranked candidate list into a coherent, buildable launch set of exactly six plated-jewelry SKUs by balancing category coverage versus depth, a price-point ladder, finish mix, collection cohesion and cross-sell/stacking, then pruning that balanced ideal against real production constraints (per-SKU MOQ, plating-run batching, launch capital) and a per-SKU contribution-margin floor — encoding every step as a decision procedure and never inventing a sell-through number, price, margin or unit count the factory has not measured.
assumptions: the ranked candidate list is inherited from kb1_signal_synthesis_ranking as a labelled [ESTIMATE] with per-candidate reliability, and is accepted here as input rather than re-derived

the launch count is fixed at exactly six SKUs by the owner's explicit instruction ('I will start with only six items') [FACT-owner brief]; this KB treats six as a hard slot budget, not a variable to optimise

per-SKU MOQ, plating-bath batch economics and unit COGS are inherited from the supply-side vertical and the S6 economics specialist as bands, never as a single measured figure; where a number is unquoted it is carried as [UNKNOWN] pending a supplier/plater quote

the audience skew (mostly young women ~18-25) and the fashion/costume tier are inherited framings from the market and owner brief, used to shape category and price choices, not asserted as measured purchase rates

finish definitions (gold-plated, vermeil, gold-filled, rhodium over sterling) follow US FTC Jewelry Guides 16 CFR Part 23 [FACT] and are carried from the S2 materials specialist; sterling silver = 92.5% Ag [FACT]

every non-fact is tagged [ESTIMATE] (with method + confidence), [METHOD] (a way to obtain the number), or [UNKNOWN]; no market size, price, margin, sell-through or demographic rate is stated as measured
exclusions: building the ranked candidate list itself and weighting the demand signals (that is kb1_signal_synthesis_ranking; this KB accepts its output)
the post-launch test-measure-cut/keep/expand loop, refresh cadence and SKU-bloat control (that is kb3_test_iterate_protocol; this KB stops at the assembled launch set and its hand-off)
deriving unit COGS, keystone/markup and the full pricing model (S6 economics kb1/kb2 own those; this KB consumes a margin floor and price-band placement as inputs)
the materials science of rhodium/gold finishes and the FTC threshold derivations (S2 materials kb2 owns those; this KB consumes the finish definitions)
the shape/motif and sizing-system taxonomies themselves (S3 form owns those; this KB consumes the sizing-return risk ranking and category producibility)
poll instrument design and paid-reach mechanics (S4 poll owns those; this KB consumes the resulting preference signal via kb1)

competency_questions.question: What makes a balanced six-SKU launch set, and how is 'balance' made checkable rather than a matter of taste?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: SLOT_ALLOCATION_MODEL states the balance as a slot allocation across the category x price-tier x finish axes, COVERAGE_VS_DEPTH_TRADEOFF states the breadth-vs-hero-depth choice, and COHERENCE_SCORECARD turns balance into a scored checklist (coverage, price spread, cohesion, cross-sell, margin) applied to a candidate six-set

competency_questions.question: How is kb1's ranked candidate list taken as the input to this KB without re-deriving or over-fitting to it?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: RANKED_CANDIDATE_INTAKE accepts the ranked list as a labelled [ESTIMATE] with per-candidate reliability, treats rank as a prior not a verdict, and names that assortment balance can legitimately override raw rank

competency_questions.question: Why exactly six SKUs, and how is the six-slot budget treated as a scarce resource that forces trade-offs?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: SIX_SLOT_MANDATE states six as the owner's fixed [FACT-owner] launch count, frames each slot as scarce, and shows that adding coverage, depth, a price tier or a finish all compete for the same six slots

competency_questions.question: How is category coverage mapped against per-category depth, and when should breadth beat depth?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: CATEGORY_COVERAGE_MAP enumerates the earring/necklace/ring/bracelet/anklet categories and the coverage-vs-depth axis, and COVERAGE_VS_DEPTH_TRADEOFF gives the rule for one-per-category breadth versus a hero category carried in depth given six slots

competency_questions.question: How is the price-point spread across the six structured, and how does a per-SKU margin floor gate it?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: PRICE_POINT_LADDER states an entry/core/hero good-better-best spread as a [METHOD] and MARGIN_FLOOR_GATE requires every SKU to clear an inherited contribution-margin floor before it earns a slot

competency_questions.question: How does the finish mix (rhodium-over-sterling versus gold-plated/vermeil) constrain the set, and what are the FTC definitions it rests on?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: FINISH_MIX_CONSTRAINT carries the 16 CFR 23 definitions [FACT] (vermeil = >=10k gold >=2.5um over sterling; rhodium a PGM over sterling; sterling = 92.5% Ag) and states how finish choice both signals the collection and drives plating-run cost

competency_questions.question: How do production constraints — per-SKU MOQ, plating-run batching and launch capital — prune the balanced candidate set to a buildable one?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: PRODUCTION_MOQ_CONSTRAINT, PLATING_RUN_BATCHING and CAPITAL_BUDGET_CONSTRAINT each state their pruning mechanism as [METHOD]/[FACT-inherited], and CONSTRAINT_PRUNING composes them into a feasibility filter that removes candidates the six-slot budget cannot fund or batch

competency_questions.question: How is collection cohesion ensured so the six read as one collection rather than six unrelated items?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: COLLECTION_COHESION states the shared-motif/finish/palette levers that make the six cohere, and COHERENCE_SCORECARD scores cohesion as one of the balance criteria

competency_questions.question: How is cross-sell and stacking designed into the set to lift average order value?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: CROSS_SELL_STACKING states the stacking/layering/set-building levers that create multi-item baskets and flags the AOV-lift claim as an [ESTIMATE]/[METHOD] to be measured post-launch, not a guaranteed number

competency_questions.question: How are the one or two hero/anchor SKUs selected from the candidate list?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: HERO_ANCHOR_SELECTION states the criteria (top demand rank + producibility + margin headroom + photogenic/shareable) for naming one or two heroes the rest of the set supports

competency_questions.question: How does the set bias toward categories that minimise sizing-driven returns?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: SIZING_RETURNS_RISK carries the inherited category return-risk ranking (rings/sized items high, earrings/necklaces low) [FACT/METHOD] and states the rule to prefer low-return categories at launch when demand is otherwise comparable

competency_questions.question: How is the final six assembled and handed off, with every soft number honestly tagged?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: LAUNCH_SET_ASSEMBLY names the final six against the slot plan and constraints, HONESTY_LEDGER separates the [FACT] anchors from the [ESTIMATE]/[UNKNOWN] soft inputs, and ASSORTMENT_HANDOFF passes the set plus its assumptions to kb3 without asserting a sell-through verdict

glossary.definition: The owner's fixed launch constraint of exactly six SKUs [FACT-owner brief], treated here as a scarce resource: every unit of category coverage, per-category depth, price tier and finish competes for the same six slots, so the assortment problem is an allocation problem, not an open-ended selection.

The trade-off between breadth (one SKU in each of several categories to cover more of the buyer's wardrobe) and depth (several variants of one hero category to win that category and enable stacking); with only six slots the two cannot both be maximised, so the KB makes the choice a rule rather than a preference.

A deliberate spread of the six across entry, core and hero price tiers so the set has an accessible entry item, a margin-rich core, and an aspirational hero; a [METHOD] for structuring the spread, with the actual prices set by the S6 economics pricing model, never invented here.

The distribution of the six across finish systems — rhodium-plated sterling (bright-white, tarnish-resistant) versus gold-plated / vermeil / gold-filled — governed by FTC 16 CFR 23 definitions [FACT]; finish both signals the collection's identity and drives plating-run cost, so it is a design lever and a production constraint at once.

The degree to which the six read as one intentional collection rather than six unrelated items, achieved through shared motif, finish family, palette and scale; cohesion raises perceived brand quality and enables cross-sell, and is scored as a balance criterion.

Designing items to be worn together (stacked rings, layered necklaces, earring pairs plus a matching pendant) so a buyer builds a multi-item basket; the AOV-lift is a plausible mechanism carried as an [ESTIMATE]/[METHOD] to be measured post-launch, never quoted as a fixed uplift.

The minimum order quantity a supplier or in-house run imposes per distinct SKU, inherited from the supply-side vertical as a band; MOQ x number-of-SKUs x unit-cost sets the launch cash commitment, so MOQ is the main reason more SKUs is not free and six is not trivially expandable.

The economics of the electroplating/PVD bath: SKUs sharing a base metal and finish can be plated in the same run, amortising bath setup, masking and chemistry, while each additional distinct finish adds a run; finish diversity thus trades design richness against plating cost [FACT-process economics].

The total working capital available for the first buy, which caps the sum over the six of (MOQ x unit COGS) plus tooling/plating setup and packaging; a hard prune that removes otherwise-attractive candidates whose MOQ x cost the launch cannot fund [METHOD], with the actual budget an owner input [UNKNOWN here].

The minimum per-unit contribution (price minus variable COGS) a SKU must clear to earn a slot, inherited from the S6 economics specialist [FACT-definition; ESTIMATE-level]; a SKU that is popular but cannot clear the floor is cut, so demand rank alone never buys a slot.

The [METHOD] that intersects the demand-balanced ideal set with the feasibility set defined by MOQ, plating-run batching, capital and the margin floor, removing candidates that cannot be built, batched, funded or sold at margin — the step that turns a wish-list into a buildable launch.

The one or two SKUs the launch is built around — highest demand rank that is also producible, margin-healthy and photogenic/shareable — which the remaining slots support through cohesion and stacking; the anchors carry the collection's story and the ad creative.

nodes.definition: Accept kb1_signal_synthesis_ranking's ranked candidate list as the input this KB assembles from, without re-deriving it: a list of candidate SKUs (category x finish x style) each carrying a demand-rank and a per-candidate reliability tag [ESTIMATE]. Treat rank as a prior, not a verdict — assortment balance, cohesion and constraints can legitimately promote a lower-ranked candidate or drop a higher-ranked one, so the intake explicitly forbids reading the ranked list as a fixed 'top-6 = the answer'. The list's reliability is inherited: if kb1 flagged a candidate's rank as thin-signal, that softness propagates into every slot decision that leans on it. No new demand number is invented here; the intake is a labelled hand-off boundary [METHOD].

included: accepting the ranked candidate list as labelled [ESTIMATE] input
rank-as-prior-not-verdict framing
propagating kb1's per-candidate reliability into slot decisions
excluded: building or weighting the ranked list (kb1 owns it)

pros.claim: Taking the ranked list as a labelled input keeps the assortment honest about where its demand belief comes from and how reliable it is
pros.example: a thin-signal poll candidate carried as rank-3 [LOW-confidence] is not treated as firmly as an on-site bestseller carried as rank-1 [MED-confidence]

cons.claim: Accepting rank as a prior means the assortment inherits any bias in kb1's signal weighting
cons.example: if the poll over-weighted a fad, the intake carries that fad into the candidate pool until cohesion/constraint steps catch it

failure_modes: reading the top-6 of the ranked list as the finished launch set and skipping the balance/constraint work
dropping kb1's reliability tags so a thin-signal candidate is treated as firmly as a strong one
acceptance_tests: the ranked candidate list is stated as accepted [ESTIMATE] input with per-candidate reliability, and rank is framed as a prior that balance and constraints can override
revisit_triggers: kb1 republishes the ranked list with new signal weights
a poll or on-site data refresh changes a candidate's rank or reliability
a candidate's reliability is downgraded to thin-signal

base.update_signal: the ranked candidate list or its reliability tags are updated

nodes.definition: Establish the hard constraint that shapes everything: the launch is exactly six SKUs, fixed by the owner ('I will start with only six items') [FACT-owner brief]. Treat six as a scarce slot budget, not a variable to optimise: every choice — an extra category, a second variant of a hero, an added price tier, an added finish — consumes one of the six and competes with every other claim on the slots. This scarcity is what makes assortment a real allocation problem: you cannot simultaneously cover five categories, run a good-better-best ladder, offer two finishes and carry a hero in depth within six slots, so the KB must trade these off explicitly. Six is small enough that each slot is a strategic bet, not a hedge.

included: six SKUs as the fixed [FACT-owner] launch count
each slot as a scarce competing resource
the impossibility of maximising coverage, ladder, finish and depth all at once in six slots
excluded: whether to expand beyond six later (kb3 test-iterate)

pros.claim: Framing six as a scarce budget forces every slot to justify itself against alternatives instead of accreting SKUs
pros.example: adding a second ring variant is explicitly costed as giving up a category or a price tier, not treated as free

cons.claim: A hard six can force out a genuinely strong seventh candidate that the data supports
cons.example: a clearly demanded anklet may have to wait for the next drop purely because the six slots are full

failure_modes: treating the six as flexible and letting SKU count creep during selection
spreading the six so thin that no category, tier or finish is actually won
acceptance_tests: six SKUs is stated as the fixed owner constraint with each slot framed as scarce, and the four-way competition (coverage, ladder, finish, depth) for the slots is named
revisit_triggers: the owner changes the launch count
kb3 test-iterate recommends expanding or contracting the set
a capital change makes more or fewer slots fundable

base.update_signal: the fixed launch count or the capital that funds it changes

nodes.definition: Map the category axis the six are allocated across: earrings (studs/hoops/drops), necklaces (chains/pendants/chokers), rings/bands, bracelets/bangles/cuffs and anklets [FACT-taxonomy, from S3 form]. For each category note its role in a plated-fashion line for the ~18-25 audience: earrings and necklaces are typically the high-frequency, low-sizing-risk, photogenic core; rings carry sizing risk; anklets are seasonal/niche. Coverage is the number of distinct categories the six touch; the map is the input to the coverage-vs-depth decision. This node classifies and characterises the categories as a [METHOD] scaffold; it asserts no purchase rates — which categories actually sell is the demand read carried in the ranked list, not invented here.

included: the five-category taxonomy and each category's role/risk profile
coverage as count-of-categories-touched
category characterisation as a [METHOD] scaffold

pros.claim: A category map with role/risk profiles lets slot allocation reason about wardrobe coverage rather than picking items ad hoc
pros.example: knowing earrings are high-frequency low-return steers at least one earring slot into most launch sets

cons.claim: Category role profiles are general framings, so a specific line can defy them
cons.example: a statement-ring-led brand would rightly over-index rings despite their sizing risk

failure_modes: asserting category purchase rates the KB is not allowed to invent
picking items without mapping which categories the six actually cover
acceptance_tests: the five categories with their role/risk profiles and coverage-as-count are stated as a [METHOD] scaffold with no invented purchase rates
revisit_triggers: the S3 form taxonomy is updated
the ranked list surfaces a category the map under-weighted
the audience framing shifts away from ~18-25 young women

base.update_signal: the category taxonomy or the audience framing changes

nodes.definition: Establish the finish axis and its dual nature as design signal and production cost. Finishes follow US FTC Jewelry Guides 16 CFR Part 23 [FACT]: gold-plated (a gold layer over base metal), vermeil (>=10k gold, >=2.5um thick, over sterling silver), gold-filled (a thicker mechanically-bonded gold layer, min 1/20 by weight), and rhodium-plated sterling — rhodium a hard, bright-white, tarnish-resistant platinum-group metal plated over sterling silver (92.5% Ag) [FACT]. Finish choice signals the collection's identity (warm gold vs bright white) and, critically, drives plating-run cost: each distinct finish is a distinct bath/run. This node carries the definitions and the design-vs-cost tension; it invents no price. Actual thickness classes and durability come from S2 materials [inherited FACT/ESTIMATE].

included: the 16 CFR 23 finish definitions [FACT]
rhodium-over-sterling as bright-white tarnish-resistant [FACT]
finish as both identity signal and per-run cost driver
excluded: the plating-run batch economics in detail (PLATING_RUN_BATCHING)
finish durability testing and thickness classes (S2 materials)

pros.claim: Anchoring finish on the FTC definitions keeps labelling honest and ties the design choice to a real cost lever
pros.example: labelling a piece 'vermeil' only when it meets the >=10k / >=2.5um over-sterling test avoids a mis-labelling exposure while flagging its higher gold cost

cons.claim: A rich finish mix strengthens the collection story but multiplies plating runs and MOQ pressure
cons.example: offering rhodium, gold-plate and vermeil across six pieces can mean three separate baths for a tiny launch

failure_modes: mis-applying an FTC finish term (e.g. calling thin gold-plate 'vermeil') and creating a labelling exposure
choosing finishes for looks alone and ignoring the per-run cost they impose
acceptance_tests: the 16 CFR 23 definitions of gold-plated/vermeil/gold-filled and rhodium-over-sterling are stated [FACT] with finish framed as both identity signal and per-run cost driver
revisit_triggers: the FTC guides are revised
S2 materials updates thickness/durability classes
a plater quote changes the per-finish run cost

base.update_signal: an FTC definition, thickness class, or per-finish run cost changes

nodes.definition: Define the price axis: spread the six across an entry / core / hero ladder (good-better-best) so the set has an accessible impulse-price entry item to convert first-time buyers, a margin-rich core that carries the P&L, and an aspirational hero that sets the brand ceiling and anchors perception. This is a [METHOD] for structuring the spread; the actual retail prices and the margin behind each are set by the S6 economics pricing model and consumed here, never invented. The ladder interacts with finish and category (a vermeil hero naturally sits high; a simple rhodium stud sits low) and with the margin floor (every rung must still clear contribution). A launch with all six at one price point forgoes both the entry conversion and the aspirational anchor.

included: the entry/core/hero good-better-best spread as a [METHOD]
the role of each rung (convert / carry margin / anchor perception)
interaction of the ladder with finish and category
excluded: setting the actual prices and margins (S6 economics)

pros.claim: A deliberate ladder gives the set an entry hook and an aspirational anchor instead of a flat undifferentiated price wall
pros.example: a low rhodium stud converts a hesitant first buyer who later trades up to the vermeil hero

cons.claim: Spreading price across six slots can dilute focus if the audience clusters tightly at one price band
cons.example: an 18-25 audience with a narrow budget may ignore a hero that eats a scarce slot

failure_modes: inventing specific prices instead of consuming the S6 pricing model
launching all six at one price point and losing both entry conversion and the aspirational anchor
acceptance_tests: the entry/core/hero ladder is stated as a [METHOD] with each rung's role and the finish/category interaction, and prices are deferred to S6 economics
revisit_triggers: the S6 pricing model changes a band or margin
the audience's price-band clustering is measured
a finish cost shift moves a rung's viable price

base.update_signal: the pricing model, audience price clustering, or a finish cost changes

nodes.definition: Carry the per-SKU minimum order quantity as the first production prune. Each distinct SKU (a unique category x finish x design) carries an MOQ from the supplier or in-house run, inherited from the supply-side vertical as a band [inherited ESTIMATE; UNKNOWN until a real quote]. MOQ is why more SKUs is not free: launch cash = sum over the six of (MOQ x unit COGS) + setup, so a high-MOQ candidate can be individually attractive yet unaffordable in a six-SKU launch. MOQ also interacts with depth: carrying a hero in two variants doubles that SKU's MOQ exposure. The node states MOQ as a pruning lever and a [METHOD] to test each candidate against ('can we fund MOQ x cost for this slot?'), never a fabricated unit count.

included: per-SKU MOQ as an inherited band and pruning lever
MOQ x unit-cost x six as the launch cash driver
MOQ interaction with per-category depth
excluded: plating-run batching that can share MOQ across finishes (PLATING_RUN_BATCHING)

pros.claim: Treating MOQ as a per-slot affordability test stops an attractive but high-MOQ candidate from silently blowing the launch budget
pros.example: a bangle with a 500-unit MOQ is tested against its slot's cash share before it is chosen, not after

cons.claim: MOQ bands are inherited and [UNKNOWN] until a real quote, so early pruning on them carries uncertainty
cons.example: a plater's true MOQ could be lower than assumed, wrongly excluding a viable candidate

failure_modes: fabricating a specific MOQ number instead of carrying the inherited band and flagging [UNKNOWN]
ignoring that carrying a hero in depth multiplies that SKU's MOQ cash
acceptance_tests: per-SKU MOQ is stated as an inherited band and per-slot affordability test, with the MOQ-x-cost-x-six cash driver and the depth interaction named, and no invented unit count
revisit_triggers: a supplier or plater quotes a real MOQ
the supply-side vertical updates its MOQ bands
a depth decision changes a SKU's MOQ exposure

base.update_signal: a real MOQ quote or an updated MOQ band arrives

nodes.definition: Carry the plating-run batching economics that makes finish diversity costly. In electroplating/PVD, SKUs sharing a base metal and a finish can be processed in the same bath/run, amortising setup, masking, rack loading and chemistry across them; each additional distinct finish (rhodium vs gold-plate vs vermeil) is a separate run with its own fixed cost [FACT-process economics, inherited from S2 materials]. For a six-SKU launch this means a set spanning three finishes can require three plating runs of tiny volume, inflating per-unit cost, while a set built on one or two finishes batches efficiently. The node states batching as a constraint that pushes toward a disciplined finish mix and rewards cohesion; it consumes the run-cost bands, inventing none.

included: shared base-metal+finish SKUs batching in one run
each distinct finish as a separate fixed-cost run
batching as a push toward a disciplined finish mix

pros.claim: Making plating runs an explicit cost aligns the finish design choice with production reality and rewards cohesion
pros.example: a launch built on rhodium-over-sterling plus one gold accent batches in two runs instead of scattering across five

cons.claim: Optimising for few runs can flatten the collection's finish variety and its perceived range
cons.example: a one-finish set batches cheaply but may read as monotonous to a browsing buyer

failure_modes: designing a finish per SKU and discovering six tiny uneconomic plating runs at costing
inventing a per-run cost instead of carrying the inherited band
acceptance_tests: shared-finish batching, each distinct finish as a separate fixed-cost run, and the push toward a disciplined finish mix are stated as inherited [FACT] process economics
revisit_triggers: S2 materials updates the plating run-cost economics
a plater quotes real per-run setup costs
the finish mix decision changes the number of runs

base.update_signal: a plating run-cost band or the finish-count changes

nodes.definition: Carry the launch capital ceiling as the binding aggregate prune. Total first-buy cash = sum over the six of (MOQ x unit COGS) + plating setup + tooling + packaging + a working-capital buffer; the owner's available launch capital caps this sum [METHOD; the actual budget is an owner input, [UNKNOWN] here]. This is the constraint that most often forces the six down from a wish-list: a balanced, cohesive, well-laddered six can still be unaffordable if its aggregate MOQ x cost exceeds the budget. The node frames capital as a hard ceiling the assembled set must fit under, and as the reason depth (which multiplies one SKU's MOQ cash) and finish diversity (which multiplies plating setup) are expensive. It quantifies nothing the owner has not supplied.

included: total first-buy cash as sum of MOQ-x-cost plus setup/tooling/packaging/buffer
capital as the binding aggregate ceiling
capital as the reason depth and finish diversity are expensive

pros.claim: A single capital ceiling forces the whole six to be costed together rather than each SKU justified in isolation
pros.example: a set whose six MOQs sum past the budget is pruned even though each SKU looked affordable alone

cons.claim: The budget is an owner [UNKNOWN] here, so the ceiling is a placeholder until the owner supplies it
cons.example: without a real budget the capital prune can only be run symbolically, not with hard numbers

failure_modes: treating each SKU's cost in isolation and blowing the aggregate budget
inventing a launch budget the owner has not stated
acceptance_tests: the total first-buy cash formula and capital as a binding aggregate ceiling are stated as a [METHOD], with the actual budget flagged an owner [UNKNOWN]
revisit_triggers: the owner supplies or changes the launch budget
an MOQ or plating-setup band updates the aggregate
a packaging or tooling cost is quoted

base.update_signal: the launch budget or an aggregate cost input changes

nodes.definition: Define the cohesion levers that make the six read as one intentional collection rather than six unrelated items. The levers: a shared motif or silhouette family, a disciplined finish family (e.g. all rhodium-white with one gold accent), a consistent scale/proportion, and a common palette/material story. Cohesion raises perceived brand quality, makes the launch photograph as a set, and is the precondition for cross-sell and stacking. This is a [METHOD] design discipline, not a measured effect; the claim that cohesion lifts conversion is plausible and carried as an [ESTIMATE] to be tested, not asserted as a number. Cohesion also aligns with plating-run batching (a shared finish is both cohesive and cheap to plate), so the design and production incentives reinforce here.

included: the shared motif/finish/scale/palette cohesion levers
cohesion as precondition for cross-sell and set photography
cohesion aligning with plating-run batching

pros.claim: Explicit cohesion levers turn 'looks like a collection' from a taste judgement into a set of checkable design choices
pros.example: requiring a shared finish family plus one motif gives a reviewer concrete criteria to accept or reject a candidate six

cons.claim: Over-tight cohesion can make the six feel repetitive and cannibalise rather than cross-sell
cons.example: six near-identical rhodium studs cohere but give a buyer little reason to buy more than one

failure_modes: asserting a specific cohesion-driven conversion lift instead of tagging it [ESTIMATE]
letting cohesion collapse into repetition that cannibalises the set
acceptance_tests: the shared motif/finish/scale/palette cohesion levers are stated as a [METHOD] with the conversion-lift claim tagged [ESTIMATE], and the batching alignment named
revisit_triggers: a post-launch test measures a cohesion-conversion effect
the finish mix or motif family changes
cohesion is found to be cannibalising rather than cross-selling

base.update_signal: a cohesion-conversion test result or a motif/finish change

nodes.definition: Design cross-sell and stacking into the set so a buyer builds a multi-item basket. Levers: stackable rings, layerable necklaces of graded lengths, an earring pair plus a coordinating pendant, and explicit 'wear-together' set framings. The mechanism for average-order-value lift is real and well-understood in accessories retail, but the size of any lift is an [ESTIMATE]/[METHOD] to be measured post-launch, never quoted as a guaranteed uplift. Stacking argues for some depth (multiples that stack) against pure category breadth, so it trades against coverage within the six slots. Cross-sell also depends on cohesion — items only stack convincingly if they share a finish/scale story — so this node builds directly on collection cohesion.

included: stacking/layering/set-framing levers for multi-item baskets
AOV lift as an [ESTIMATE]/[METHOD] to be measured, not quoted
stacking's tension with pure category breadth
excluded: the cohesion levers stacking depends on (COLLECTION_COHESION)

pros.claim: Designing for stacking creates a mechanism for larger baskets without adding slots beyond the six
pros.example: three graded-length necklaces that layer let one buyer purchase all three as a look

cons.claim: Stacking consumes slots on depth that could have gone to category coverage, and its AOV payoff is unproven at launch
cons.example: two stackable rings win the ring category but leave no slot for a bracelet

failure_modes: quoting a specific AOV uplift instead of tagging it [ESTIMATE] to be measured
building stackers that do not share a finish/scale story and so do not actually stack
acceptance_tests: the stacking/layering/set levers are stated with AOV lift tagged [ESTIMATE]/[METHOD], and the depth-vs-coverage tension named
revisit_triggers: a post-launch basket-size measurement lands
the coverage-vs-depth decision changes the room for stackers
cohesion changes whether the items actually stack

base.update_signal: a basket-size measurement or a depth-allocation change

nodes.definition: Give the rule for the central trade-off: with six slots, breadth (one SKU per category, covering more of the wardrobe) competes with depth (multiple variants of a hero category, winning it and enabling stacking). The [METHOD]: default to breadth-with-one-hero — cover the two-to-three highest-demand, lowest-return categories once each, then invest the remaining one-to-two slots as depth behind the single highest-conviction hero. Go deeper only when the ranked-list signal for a hero category is strong and reliable and stacking is the intended AOV mechanism; stay broad when demand is diffuse or thin-signal. This node consumes the category map and the six-slot budget and produces the breadth/depth split that the slot allocation then fills.

included: breadth vs depth as competing claims on six slots
the breadth-with-one-hero default rule
when to go deeper vs stay broad based on signal strength

pros.claim: A stated breadth-vs-depth rule stops the six from either spreading uselessly thin or over-committing to one unproven category
pros.example: covering earrings+necklace+ring once then doubling the earring hero gives both wardrobe reach and a category to win

cons.claim: The rule is a heuristic; a genuinely dominant single category could justify more depth than the default allows
cons.example: if the ranked list overwhelmingly favours hoops, a three-deep hoop hero might beat breadth

failure_modes: spreading all six as pure breadth and winning no category
over-committing depth to a thin-signal hero the data does not support
acceptance_tests: the breadth-vs-depth competition and the breadth-with-one-hero default (deeper only on strong reliable signal) are stated as a [METHOD]
revisit_triggers: the ranked list's signal strength for a hero category changes
the stacking strategy changes the value of depth
post-launch data favours breadth or depth

base.update_signal: the hero-signal strength or the stacking strategy changes

nodes.definition: Carry the sizing-return risk ranking as a launch-selection bias. Categories differ sharply in sizing-driven returns: rings and any sized/fit-critical item carry high exchange/return risk, while earrings (especially studs), most necklaces and adjustable pieces carry low risk [FACT/METHOD, inherited from S3 form kb3]. For a first launch — where a return spike burns scarce cash and a thin operation cannot absorb heavy reverse logistics — the rule is to prefer low-sizing-return categories when demand is otherwise comparable, and to design sizing risk down (adjustable chains, standard hoop diameters, a clear ring-size guide) when a sized category must be carried. This node biases the assortment toward operational survivability; it invents no return-rate number, carrying the inherited ranking and method.

included: the category sizing-return risk ranking [inherited FACT/METHOD]
prefer-low-return-categories-at-launch rule
designing sizing risk down when a sized category is carried

pros.claim: Biasing the first launch toward low-return categories protects the scarce cash a return spike would burn
pros.example: leading with studs and an adjustable necklace over a sized ring reduces launch reverse-logistics exposure

cons.claim: Avoiding sized categories can forgo genuine demand for rings the audience wants
cons.example: an audience that mostly wants stacking rings is under-served by a return-averse earring-led set

failure_modes: inventing a return-rate percentage instead of carrying the inherited ranking
loading the launch with sized items and getting buried in exchanges early
acceptance_tests: the category sizing-return ranking, the prefer-low-return-at-launch rule, and the design-risk-down mitigation are stated with no invented return rate
revisit_triggers: S3 form updates the sizing-return ranking
post-launch return data measures the real rates
a sizing-risk-down design (adjustable/standard sizing) is adopted

base.update_signal: the sizing-return ranking or measured return data changes

nodes.definition: Impose the per-SKU contribution-margin floor as a hard gate on slot eligibility. Contribution margin = price minus variable COGS (base metal + plating consumption + findings + labour + packaging), inherited from the S6 economics specialist [FACT-definition; ESTIMATE-level, [UNKNOWN] exact figures until costed]. The rule: every candidate must clear the floor to earn one of the six slots; a popular but thin-margin candidate is cut or re-engineered (value engineering: base-metal choice, plating-thickness tuning, batching) before it takes a slot. This gate is what stops demand rank from buying a slot on its own — a SKU that cannot clear contribution drains the launch even if it sells. The floor value itself is set by S6, consumed here, never invented.

included: contribution margin as price minus variable COGS [inherited]
the floor as a hard slot-eligibility gate
re-engineer-or-cut a thin-margin popular candidate
excluded: deriving COGS and the floor value (S6 economics)

pros.claim: A hard margin floor prevents a popular-but-unprofitable SKU from consuming a scarce slot and draining the launch
pros.example: a much-liked but thin-margin vermeil piece is re-engineered to a rhodium finish to clear the floor before it earns a slot

cons.claim: A strict floor can cut a strategic entry item whose role is conversion rather than margin
cons.example: a low-margin loss-leader stud that pulls first buyers might be wrongly gated out

failure_modes: letting demand rank buy a slot for a SKU that cannot clear the contribution floor
inventing a margin figure instead of consuming the S6 floor
acceptance_tests: contribution margin as price minus variable COGS, the floor as a hard slot gate, and the re-engineer-or-cut rule are stated with the floor value deferred to S6
revisit_triggers: S6 economics updates the COGS or the floor
a value-engineering change moves a candidate's margin across the floor
a strategic entry item is exempted by explicit decision

base.update_signal: the COGS, margin floor, or a value-engineering change

nodes.definition: Compose the production and margin constraints into one feasibility filter that turns the demand-balanced wish-list into a buildable set. The [METHOD]: intersect the balanced candidate ideal with the feasibility set defined by per-SKU MOQ (fundable?), plating-run batching (batches into few runs?), aggregate launch capital (fits the ceiling?) and the contribution-margin floor (clears margin?). A candidate that fails any of these is pruned or re-engineered before it can hold a slot. The order matters: apply the cheap, decisive prunes first (margin floor, gross MOQ affordability) then the aggregate capital fit, iterating — dropping the weakest surviving candidate and re-checking capital until the six fit. This node is the hinge that answers 'how constraints prune the candidate list' [METHOD].

included: intersecting the balanced ideal with the MOQ/batching/capital/margin feasibility set
cheap-decisive-prunes-first ordering with iterative capital re-check
prune-or-re-engineer a failing candidate
excluded: the individual constraints' definitions (their own nodes)
the final naming of the six (LAUNCH_SET_ASSEMBLY)

pros.claim: A single composed feasibility filter makes 'buildable' a checkable intersection rather than an afterthought discovered at costing
pros.example: a balanced six that fails the capital ceiling is iteratively pruned to a feasible six before design work is committed

cons.claim: Iterative pruning can drift the set away from the demand-optimal balance if constraints bite hard
cons.example: a tight budget may force out the best hero and leave a merely feasible, less compelling six

failure_modes: applying constraints in the wrong order and re-doing capital fit repeatedly
pruning to feasibility while silently abandoning the balance and cohesion criteria
acceptance_tests: the feasibility intersection (MOQ, batching, capital, margin), the cheap-prunes-first-then-capital-fit ordering, and prune-or-re-engineer are stated as a [METHOD]
revisit_triggers: any constraint band (MOQ, run cost, capital, margin) updates
the balanced ideal set changes
a re-engineered candidate re-enters the feasible set

base.update_signal: a constraint band or the balanced ideal set changes

nodes.definition: Select the one or two hero/anchor SKUs the launch is built around. Criteria: highest demand rank from the intake that is also (a) producible at the owner's scale, (b) margin-healthy above the floor with headroom, and (c) photogenic/shareable for the paid-social creative the venture depends on. The hero carries the collection's story, headlines the ads, and gives the price ladder its aspirational top or its conversion entry depending on strategy; the remaining slots support it through cohesion and stacking. Limit to one or two — a launch with three heroes has none. This node consumes the intake and the coverage-vs-depth split and names the anchors the rest of the assortment orbits; it invents no popularity or conversion figure, using inherited rank and producibility.

included: the hero criteria: top rank + producible + margin headroom + photogenic
the hero carrying the story and the ad creative
limit to one or two heroes

pros.claim: Naming one or two anchors gives the launch a focal point for creative and a spine for the supporting slots
pros.example: a photogenic rhodium hoop hero headlines the ads while a pendant and stud are built to cohere with it

cons.claim: Betting the launch on one or two heroes concentrates risk if the anchor under-performs
cons.example: if the hero flops, the supporting cohesion offers less independent pull

failure_modes: choosing a hero on demand rank alone without checking producibility or margin headroom
naming three-plus heroes so the launch has no real focal point
acceptance_tests: the hero criteria (top rank + producible + margin headroom + photogenic) and the one-or-two-heroes limit are stated, using inherited rank not an invented figure
revisit_triggers: the intake rank of the hero candidate changes
a producibility or margin check fails the chosen hero
post-launch data shows the hero under-performing

base.update_signal: the hero candidate's rank, producibility, or margin changes

nodes.definition: Allocate the six slots across the three design axes — category, price tier and finish — into a concrete slot plan. The [METHOD]: lay the six against the breadth/depth split from the trade-off node, place each slot on the price ladder (target roughly an entry, a cluster of core, and a hero rung), and assign finishes consistent with the batching discipline (favour one dominant finish family plus at most one accent). The output is a slot grid: e.g. slot1 = entry rhodium stud, slot2-3 = core rhodium necklace + hoop (hero-adjacent), slot4 = core gold-accent ring, slot5-6 = depth behind the hero — illustrative only, tagged [METHOD], with actual SKUs filled from the pruned candidate pool. This node is the constructive answer to 'what makes a balanced six' before scoring.

included: allocating six slots across category x price x finish into a slot grid
aligning finish assignment with batching discipline
the grid as an illustrative [METHOD], not fixed SKUs

pros.claim: A slot grid makes the balance concrete and auditable across all three axes at once
pros.example: seeing the six laid on category x price x finish immediately reveals a gap (e.g. no entry-price item) to fix

cons.claim: A grid built before the feasibility prune may need reshuffling once constraints bite
cons.example: a slot planned as vermeil may have to drop to rhodium after the plating-run and capital prune

failure_modes: presenting the illustrative grid as a fixed SKU list rather than a [METHOD] scaffold
allocating slots on one axis (category) while ignoring price and finish balance
acceptance_tests: the six-slot grid across category x price x finish, aligned with batching discipline and tagged [METHOD], is stated with the breadth/depth split applied
revisit_triggers: the breadth/depth split or price ladder changes
the feasibility prune forces a slot reshuffle
a finish reassignment changes the grid

base.update_signal: an axis input (category, price, finish, depth) or the prune changes the grid

nodes.definition: Turn 'balance' into a scored checklist applied to a candidate six-set so the choice is defensible, not a matter of taste. The scorecard rates the set on: category coverage (does it reach the intended wardrobe breadth?), price spread (entry/core/hero present?), collection cohesion (shared motif/finish/scale?), cross-sell/stacking (does it build multi-item baskets?), demand alignment (do the slots reflect the ranked signal?), and margin health (all clear the floor with a healthy blended margin?). Each criterion is scored and the weakest flagged for a fix; a candidate six that scores poorly on a criterion is revised before assembly. Scores are a [METHOD] decision aid using inherited/estimated inputs, not measured outcomes — the scorecard ranks candidate sets against each other, it does not predict sales.

included: scoring a candidate six on coverage/price/cohesion/cross-sell/demand/margin
flagging the weakest criterion for a fix
the scorecard as a comparative [METHOD], not a sales prediction

pros.claim: A scorecard makes assortment balance a defensible, comparable judgement across candidate sets
pros.example: two candidate sixes are compared criterion-by-criterion and the one with a missing entry-price rung is revised

cons.claim: Scoring inherited/estimated inputs can create false precision if the weights are treated as measured
cons.example: a set that scores 0.8 is not 'measurably better' than 0.75 given the soft inputs

failure_modes: treating scorecard numbers as measured outcomes rather than a comparative aid
scoring only the easy criteria (coverage) and skipping margin or cohesion
acceptance_tests: the six scoring criteria (coverage, price spread, cohesion, cross-sell, demand alignment, margin health) and the weakest-criterion-fix loop are stated as a comparative [METHOD]
revisit_triggers: a scoring input (cohesion, price, margin, demand) is updated
post-launch data validates or invalidates a criterion weight
a candidate set is revised and re-scored

base.update_signal: a scoring input or a validated criterion weight changes

nodes.definition: Assemble and name the final six: take the pruned, feasible candidate pool, apply the slot allocation and the coherence scorecard, and commit the specific six SKUs (each a category x finish x design x price-tier x hero/support role) that best satisfy the balance criteria within the constraints. Record for each slot its rationale (which criterion and which demand signal it serves) and its inherited assumptions (MOQ band, margin, reliability). The assembly is a decision, not a prediction: it states what to build and why, tagged so that every soft input (demand rank, MOQ, margin) is visibly [ESTIMATE]/[UNKNOWN]. This is the KB's central deliverable — a defensible, buildable launch set of six — and it explicitly does not claim the six will sell, only that they are the best-balanced feasible set given current signals.

included: committing the specific six with per-slot rationale and inherited assumptions
the set as a defensible decision, not a sales prediction
visible tagging of every soft input
excluded: the honesty ledger that catalogs the tags (HONESTY_LEDGER)

pros.claim: A committed six with per-slot rationale gives the venture a buildable, auditable launch plan instead of a vague shortlist
pros.example: each of the six carries a one-line why (category served, signal, role) a reviewer can challenge

cons.claim: Committing the six freezes decisions on soft signals that may shift before production
cons.example: a demand rank that moves after the poll refresh could change a slot already committed

failure_modes: presenting the assembled six as a sales forecast rather than a best-balanced feasible decision
committing SKUs without recording their inherited assumptions and tags
acceptance_tests: the final six are named with per-slot rationale and inherited assumptions, framed as a defensible decision not a prediction, with every soft input tagged
revisit_triggers: a demand or constraint input shifts before production commit
the scorecard flags a weak slot after assembly
kb3 test-iterate returns a cut/keep signal

base.update_signal: a demand or constraint input or a scorecard flag changes the committed six

nodes.definition: Enforce the honesty discipline across the launch set so the venture trusts the method but not fabricated numbers. Solid [FACT] (cited, load-bearing): the six-SKU count (owner instruction); the FTC 16 CFR 23 finish definitions (vermeil >=10k >=2.5um over sterling; rhodium a tarnish-resistant PGM; sterling 92.5% Ag); the plating-run batching economics (shared finish batches, each finish a run); the sizing-return risk ordering (sized items high, studs/necklaces low); contribution-margin as price minus variable COGS. Soft [ESTIMATE/UNKNOWN]: every demand rank (inherited from kb1's signals); every MOQ and unit-cost band ([UNKNOWN] until a supplier/plater quote); the launch capital budget (owner [UNKNOWN]); the AOV lift from stacking and the conversion lift from cohesion (unmeasured [ESTIMATE]). The assembled six is a best-balanced feasible decision, robust in method, soft in every quantity — never a claim the set will sell.

included: the [FACT] anchors (count, FTC defs, batching, return ordering, margin def)
the [ESTIMATE]/[UNKNOWN] soft inputs (ranks, MOQ, cost, budget, AOV/conversion lifts)
the set as method-robust but quantity-soft, never a sales claim
excluded: the substantive assortment content (the other nodes)

pros.claim: A single ledger separating firm anchors from soft inputs keeps the launch decision trusted while flagging every quantity as unmeasured
pros.example: tagging the FTC finish defs [FACT] but the MOQ and demand rank [ESTIMATE]/[UNKNOWN] tells a reader exactly what to trust

cons.claim: Heavy tagging can read as hedging when a stakeholder wants a single confident answer
cons.example: an owner wanting a firm 'these six will sell' must accept a best-feasible decision with soft quantities

failure_modes: promoting a soft demand rank or MOQ band to a measured claim
hardening the unmeasured AOV/conversion lifts into quoted percentages
acceptance_tests: the [FACT] anchors and the [ESTIMATE]/[UNKNOWN] soft inputs are enumerated, and the set is framed as method-robust but quantity-soft, not a sales claim
revisit_triggers: a soft input is hardened by a real quote or measurement
a [FACT] anchor (e.g. an FTC definition) is revised
an AOV/conversion lift is measured post-launch

base.update_signal: a soft input is hardened or a [FACT] anchor is revised

nodes.definition: Compose the segment's hand-off to kb3_test_iterate_protocol and stop cleanly. Deliver the assembled six with, per slot: its rationale, its inherited assumptions (demand rank + reliability, MOQ band, contribution margin, sizing-return class, finish/plating run), and the specific measurements kb3 should watch (sell-through, return rate, contribution realised). State the binding conditions the assortment passes on: re-confirm MOQ and unit cost with a real supplier/plater quote before committing capital; confirm the launch budget covers the aggregate; and treat the six as a testable hypothesis, not a fixed catalogue. This KB owns whether the six are a balanced, buildable, cohesive set; it does NOT own the post-launch cut/keep/expand decision or the refresh cadence (kb3), nor the sales outcome. A clean boundary keeps the assortment from overstepping into the measurement loop.

included: the six with per-slot rationale, assumptions and the metrics kb3 should watch
the binding conditions (re-confirm MOQ/cost, confirm budget, treat as hypothesis)
the clean boundary before the cut/keep/expand loop
excluded: the post-launch measurement and cut/keep decision (kb3)

pros.claim: A clean hand-off gives kb3 a testable six with the assumptions and metrics it needs, without claiming the outcome
pros.example: passing each slot's sell-through-and-return metrics lets kb3 run the keep/cut loop on a documented base

cons.claim: The hand-off carries soft assumptions kb3 must re-confirm, so the base is a hypothesis not a proven set
cons.example: an MOQ band that changes at quote could alter which slots survive before kb3 even measures them

failure_modes: letting the assortment drift into the post-launch cut/keep decision kb3 owns
handing off the six without the per-slot assumptions and watch-metrics kb3 needs
acceptance_tests: the six with per-slot rationale/assumptions/watch-metrics, the three binding conditions, and the clean pre-measurement boundary are stated
revisit_triggers: a supplier/plater quote or the budget re-confirms an assumption
kb3 requests a different metric or a slot revision
a demand or constraint input changes before launch

base.update_signal: an assumption re-confirmation or a kb3 metric/slot request changes the hand-off

the margin floor gates each rung of the price ladder
MOQ affordability is one prune the feasibility filter composes

the margin floor is one prune the feasibility filter composes

the slot grid assigns finishes across the six

maximising category breadth and carrying a hero in depth both claim the same six slots and cannot both be maximised
edges.resolution_rule: apply the breadth-with-one-hero default: cover the two-to-three highest-demand low-return categories once, then invest remaining slots as depth behind the single highest-conviction hero; go deeper only on strong, reliable signal

edges.why_related: a richer finish mix strengthens the collection story but multiplies plating runs and per-unit cost
edges.resolution_rule: favour one dominant finish family plus at most one accent finish; add a third finish only if a hero's demand and margin clearly justify its separate plating run

edges.why_related: a full good-better-best spread wants a costly hero while the capital ceiling caps how much MOQ-x-cost the six can carry
edges.resolution_rule: keep the ladder but size the hero's MOQ to fit the aggregate capital ceiling; if the budget cannot fund the hero rung, compress the ladder toward entry/core rather than breach capital

edges.why_related: designing depth for stacking consumes slots that pure category coverage would spend on breadth
edges.resolution_rule: resolve via the coverage-vs-depth default: spend depth on stacking only behind the chosen hero, keeping enough breadth to cover the top low-return categories once each

edges.why_related: a top-ranked popular candidate can fail the contribution-margin floor, so demand rank and margin can disagree on whether it earns a slot
edges.resolution_rule: the margin floor is a hard gate: a popular candidate that cannot clear contribution is re-engineered (value engineering) or cut; demand rank never buys a slot on its own

edges.why_related: raising per-SKU MOQ directly raises the aggregate first-buy cash the capital ceiling must cover

conflict_axes.name: category_breadth_vs_hero_depth
conflict_axes.description: Covering more categories (breadth) versus carrying one category in depth (a hero with variants) both claim the scarce six slots and cannot both be maximised.
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: default to breadth-with-one-hero: cover the top low-return categories once, then invest remaining slots as depth behind the single highest-conviction hero

conflict_axes.name: finish_richness_vs_plating_run_cost
conflict_axes.description: A richer finish mix (rhodium + gold-plate + vermeil) strengthens the collection story but each distinct finish is a separate plating run, inflating per-unit cost on a tiny launch.
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: one dominant finish family plus at most one accent; add a third finish only when a hero's demand and margin justify its own run

conflict_axes.name: price_spread_vs_capital_ceiling
conflict_axes.description: A full good-better-best ladder wants a costly aspirational hero, but the launch capital ceiling caps how much aggregate MOQ-x-cost the six can carry.
poles: run a full price ladder with a hero
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: keep the ladder but size the hero's MOQ to the ceiling; if unaffordable, compress toward entry/core rather than breach capital

conflict_axes.name: demand_rank_vs_margin_floor
conflict_axes.description: A top-ranked, popular candidate may fail the per-SKU contribution-margin floor, so demand and margin disagree on whether it earns a slot.
poles: give the popular candidate a slot
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: the margin floor is a hard gate; re-engineer the popular candidate to clear contribution or cut it — rank never buys a slot alone

conflict_axes.name: demand_rank_vs_sizing_return_risk
conflict_axes.description: The highest-demand category may be a sized, high-return one (rings) while a first launch needs to protect scarce cash from a return spike.
poles: follow raw demand into sized categories
bias toward low-return categories at launch
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: prefer low-sizing-return categories when demand is comparable; if a sized category is demanded, design its sizing risk down (adjustable/standard sizing, size guide)

conflict_axes.name: cohesion_vs_stacking_variety
conflict_axes.description: Tight cohesion makes the six read as one collection, but if they are too similar they cannibalise instead of cross-selling; enough variety is needed to stack.
poles: vary enough to stack and cross-sell
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: cohere on finish/palette/scale while varying category and role so items complement and stack rather than duplicate

conflict_axes.name: raw_rank_fidelity_vs_assortment_balance
conflict_axes.description: Following the ranked list's top-6 literally maximises fidelity to the demand signal but can produce an unbalanced, incohesive, or infeasible set.
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: treat rank as a prior; let balance, cohesion and constraints promote or drop candidates, documenting each deviation from raw rank

conflict_axes.name: single_confident_set_vs_honest_hypothesis
conflict_axes.description: Stakeholders want a confident 'these six will sell' while the evidence supports only a best-balanced feasible decision on soft, unmeasured inputs.
poles: carry the six as a tagged hypothesis
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: commit the six as a defensible decision with every quantity tagged [ESTIMATE]/[UNKNOWN], to be tested by kb3, not claimed as a sales forecast

conflict_axes.name: feasibility_pruning_vs_demand_optimality
conflict_axes.description: Pruning hard to fit MOQ, batching and capital guarantees a buildable set but can drift it away from the demand-optimal balance.
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: prune the weakest candidate first and re-check balance each iteration; if feasibility forces out the hero, revisit capital or re-engineer before abandoning balance

edge_cases.description: The ranked list's literal top-6 are all in one category (e.g. six earring styles), giving zero wardrobe coverage
edge_cases.trigger: a demand signal heavily concentrated in a single category
edge_cases.mitigation: apply the breadth-with-one-hero rule: keep the strongest one-to-three earring variants as the hero and spend remaining slots on adjacent low-return categories

edge_cases.description: A top-demand candidate cannot clear the contribution-margin floor at any viable price
edge_cases.trigger: a popular candidate whose COGS leaves no margin at the audience's price band
edge_cases.mitigation: value-engineer it (base-metal/finish/plating-thickness) to clear the floor, or cut it and promote the next candidate; never seat it on rank alone

edge_cases.description: The balanced ideal six's aggregate MOQ-x-cost exceeds the launch capital ceiling
edge_cases.trigger: the sum of per-SKU MOQ cash plus setup breaches the budget
edge_cases.mitigation: iteratively drop the weakest surviving slot and re-check capital; compress finish/depth to lower aggregate MOQ before breaching the ceiling

edge_cases.mitigation: carry rings only with sizing risk designed down (adjustable/open bands, standard sizing, a clear size guide) or defer them to a later drop

edge_cases.description: The six are so tightly cohesive they cannibalise instead of cross-selling

edge_cases.description: The stacking AOV lift or the cohesion conversion lift is quoted as a firm percentage in a plan

edge_cases.mitigation: tag both lifts [ESTIMATE]/[METHOD] to be measured post-launch by kb3; never quote a fixed uplift

edge_cases.description: A slot's MOQ band is [UNKNOWN] and a placeholder number is hardened into the capital plan

workflow.description: Lay the six on a category x price x finish grid consistent with the breadth/depth split and batching discipline
workflow.gate: the six-slot grid across the three axes is stated as a [METHOD] scaffold, not fixed SKUs

workflow.description: Rate the candidate six on coverage, price spread, cohesion, cross-sell, demand alignment and margin health, fixing the weakest
workflow.gate: the six criteria are scored as a comparative [METHOD] and the weakest criterion flagged for a fix

workflow.description: Commit the specific six from the pruned pool with per-slot rationale and inherited assumptions, framed as a decision not a prediction
workflow.gate: the six are named with per-slot rationale/assumptions and every soft input tagged

workflow.description: Separate the [FACT] anchors from the [ESTIMATE]/[UNKNOWN] soft inputs and flag the set as method-robust, quantity-soft
workflow.gate: the [FACT] anchors and the soft inputs are enumerated and the no-sales-claim framing stated

workflow.description: Pass the six with per-slot assumptions and watch-metrics plus the binding conditions to kb3, stopping before the cut/keep loop
workflow.gate: the six, their assumptions/watch-metrics, the three binding conditions and the clean pre-measurement boundary are stated

dominance_rules.rule: The contribution-margin floor dominates demand rank for slot eligibility
dominance_rules.rationale: a SKU that cannot clear contribution drains the launch even if it is popular
dominance_rules.trigger: a top-ranked candidate fails the margin floor
dominance_rules.action: re-engineer it to clear the floor or cut it; never seat it on rank alone

dominance_rules.rule: The capital ceiling dominates the ideal balanced set
dominance_rules.rationale: an unaffordable six cannot be built regardless of how balanced it is
dominance_rules.trigger: the aggregate MOQ-x-cost exceeds the launch budget
dominance_rules.action: iteratively prune the weakest slot and compress finish/depth until the six fit the ceiling

dominance_rules.rule: The six-slot budget dominates the urge to add SKUs
dominance_rules.rationale: six is the owner's fixed launch count and each added SKU multiplies MOQ cash
dominance_rules.trigger: a seventh attractive candidate pressures the set
dominance_rules.action: hold at six; defer the extra to kb3's next drop rather than expanding the launch

dominance_rules.rule: Plating-run batching dominates finish variety for a tiny launch
dominance_rules.rationale: each distinct finish is a separate fixed-cost run that inflates per-unit cost at low volume
dominance_rules.trigger: the set spans three or more finishes
dominance_rules.action: consolidate to one dominant finish plus at most one accent unless a hero clearly justifies its own run

dominance_rules.rule: Low sizing-return categories dominate at launch when demand is comparable
dominance_rules.rationale: a return spike burns scarce launch cash a thin operation cannot absorb
dominance_rules.trigger: a sized high-return category competes with a low-return one at similar demand
dominance_rules.action: prefer the low-return category or design the sized item's risk down before carrying it

dominance_rules.rule: Assortment balance dominates raw rank fidelity
dominance_rules.rationale: the literal top-6 can be unbalanced, incohesive or infeasible
dominance_rules.trigger: following raw rank produces zero coverage or breaks cohesion/feasibility
dominance_rules.action: treat rank as a prior and reshape for balance, documenting each deviation

dominance_rules.rule: The tested-hypothesis framing dominates any confident sales claim
dominance_rules.rationale: every quantity behind the six is inherited-soft or unmeasured
dominance_rules.trigger: the six are about to be stated as a sales forecast
dominance_rules.action: present them as a best-balanced feasible decision with tagged quantities, to be validated by kb3

dominance_rules.rule: A real supplier/plater quote dominates an inherited MOQ/cost band
dominance_rules.rationale: capital commitment on a placeholder band risks a mis-sized launch
dominance_rules.trigger: capital is about to be committed on an [UNKNOWN] MOQ band
dominance_rules.action: re-confirm MOQ and unit cost with a real quote before committing capital

anti_rework_rules.rule: Take kb1's ranked list as a labelled prior with reliability tags from the first step
anti_rework_rules.prevents: over-fitting the launch to a thin-signal rank that later has to be unwound

anti_rework_rules.rule: Run the margin floor and gross MOQ affordability as the first, cheap prunes before detailed design
anti_rework_rules.prevents: designing and cohering a set that a late margin or capital check forces to be rebuilt

anti_rework_rules.rule: Fix the finish mix to one dominant family plus at most one accent before allocating slots
anti_rework_rules.prevents: discovering three uneconomic plating runs at costing and re-selecting finishes

anti_rework_rules.rule: Confirm the launch capital ceiling and per-SKU MOQ bands before committing the slot grid
anti_rework_rules.prevents: committing a balanced grid the budget cannot fund and re-pruning after design

anti_rework_rules.rule: Bias toward low sizing-return categories at launch unless a sized item's risk is designed down first
anti_rework_rules.prevents: a first-launch return spike that burns cash and forces an emergency assortment cut

anti_rework_rules.rule: Tag every demand rank, MOQ, cost, budget and lift as [ESTIMATE]/[UNKNOWN] when first used
anti_rework_rules.prevents: a soft quantity circulating as measured and having to be retracted downstream

anti_rework_rules.rule: Apply the FTC finish definitions to labelling before naming a finish 'vermeil' or 'gold-filled'
anti_rework_rules.prevents: a mis-labelling exposure discovered after packaging and copy are produced

anti_rework_rules.rule: Record each slot's rationale and assumptions at assembly, not after
anti_rework_rules.prevents: kb3 receiving an undocumented six it cannot test and having to reconstruct the rationale

anti_rework_rules.rule: Treat the six as a testable hypothesis handed to kb3, not a final catalogue
anti_rework_rules.prevents: locking the assortment against the measured cut/keep/expand signal and re-doing the launch

iteration_protocol.trigger: kb1 republishes the ranked candidate list or a poll/on-site refresh changes a rank or reliability
iteration_protocol.action: re-intake the candidates and re-run slot allocation and the scorecard

iteration_protocol.trigger: a real supplier/plater quote fixes an MOQ, unit cost or plating-run cost
iteration_protocol.action: tighten the constraint bands and re-run the feasibility prune and capital fit

iteration_protocol.trigger: the owner supplies or changes the launch capital budget
iteration_protocol.action: re-run the capital prune and re-check whether the balanced six still fit

iteration_protocol.trigger: the S6 economics COGS or margin floor is updated
iteration_protocol.action: re-gate each slot against the new floor and re-engineer or cut failing candidates

iteration_protocol.trigger: the S3 form sizing-return ranking or a sizing-risk-down design changes
iteration_protocol.action: re-bias the category selection and update the hand-off's return assumptions

iteration_protocol.trigger: kb3 test-iterate returns a cut/keep/expand signal after launch
iteration_protocol.action: revise the committed six and re-hand-off the updated set

iteration_protocol.trigger: a post-launch measurement quantifies a stacking-AOV or cohesion-conversion lift
iteration_protocol.action: replace the [ESTIMATE] lift with the measured value and re-score cross-sell and cohesion

priority_rationale: The candidate intake, six-slot mandate, category map, finish axis and price ladder come first because every downstream choice allocates the accepted candidates across those fixed axes and the scarce six slots; the production and margin constraints (MOQ, plating-run batching, capital, margin floor) and the design-balance nodes (coverage-vs-depth, cohesion, cross-sell, sizing risk) come next because they define the feasibility set and the balance criteria; the constraint-pruning, hero selection, slot allocation and coherence scorecard then intersect balance with feasibility and rank the candidate sets; and the assembly, honesty ledger and hand-off come last because they commit the final six, tag every soft quantity, and pass a testable hypothesis to kb3 without claiming a sales outcome.
